sentences: Ten tall panels stand side by side like a wall.
Across them run old bronze vessels and branches of flowering plants, and everything is painted in black ink alone.
This is a ten-panel folding screen attributed to Jang Seung-eop, a painter of the last years of the Joseon dynasty.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York owns it and dates it to 1894.
The museum calls it attributed, so it does not claim for certain that he painted it.
Think about its size.
It stands about 196 centimetres high, taller than most adults, and opened out it is over four metres wide.
Folded, it is only about 43 centimetres across.
The Korean name of the genre means vessels and cut branches.
It is a kind of still life that shows ancient bronze or ceramic pots with flowering branches, fruit and vegetables.
Its roots lie in Chinese pictures of antiques and objects from a scholar's study.
The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture says Jang created this form after studying vessel and flower paintings popular in the Chinese cities of Yangzhou and Shanghai.
The painter Kim Yong-jun also wrote that Owon was the one who spread such pictures in Korea.
Each object carries a meaning.
Ancient bronzes stood for the good taste of a learned scholar.
Flowers, fruit and strange rocks stood for wealth, long life and many sons.
So the genre was loved everywhere, from the royal palace to ordinary homes.
Now look at the vessels.
Jang often added colour to his ink, but the museum lists this screen as ink on paper only.
Without colour, the weight and shine of the metal must come from the dark and pale tones of the ink.
Move your eyes to the flowering branches.
The encyclopedia names bold, free brushwork and a zigzag layout packed with objects as marks of Jang's still lifes.
Walk slowly from panel to panel and see whether you can find them here.
Jang Seung-eop was born in 1843 and died in 1897.
He lost his parents early and grew up poor.
Living in the house of Yi Eung-heon, a government interpreter, he could study old masterpieces.
Around the age of forty he was called to paint for the royal court.
Stories say he loved drink and hated rules.
Today he is remembered with Danwon and Hyewon as one of the Three Wons of Joseon painting.
His style passed to An Jung-sik and Jo Seok-jin, and in the early twentieth century this kind of still life became very popular in Korean painting.
The screen came to the museum as a gift in 2014.
Step back and take in all ten panels at once.
Old vessels and fresh blossoms meet on one long surface and become a wall of good wishes.
Today, try placing a single flower beside something old you have kept for years.
